get.summary:
`@Get()` with no argument = the controller's base path.

The return value is a plain object. Nest's built-in serialiser turns it
into JSON and sets `Content-Type: application/json` - no `res.json()`.
Status defaults to 200 for GET and 201 for POST (change it with
@HttpCode()).

A liveness probe: "is this process up and able to answer?"

`@HttpCode(HttpStatus.OK)` is redundant on a GET (200 is already the
default) but it is here to make the decorator visible, and to note the
rule: a health endpoint must be CHEAP. It must not touch the database,
because a liveness probe that fails when the database is slow will make
Kubernetes restart perfectly healthy pods, turning a database blip into an
application outage.

Phase 18 replaces this with @nestjs/terminus and splits liveness (is the
process alive?) from readiness (can it serve traffic right now?) - the
distinction that prevents exactly that outage.

post.summary: "Sign out everywhere" - what a user clicks after a suspicious-login alert.

get.summary:
"Who am I?" - the endpoint every frontend calls on boot.

Note it READS FROM THE DATABASE rather than returning the token's claims.
The token is a snapshot up to 15 minutes old; this endpoint exists
precisely so a client can see the CURRENT name and role. Returning the
token's claims would make a just-promoted user look unpromoted until they
logged out - and this is the one route where paying for a query is
obviously right.

patch.summary:
SELF-SERVICE PROFILE EDIT.

PHASE 8 moved this out of `PATCH /users/:id`, which is now admin-only. The
id is not a parameter at all - it comes from the token, so there is no
"can this user edit that user?" question to get wrong. An endpoint that
cannot express the unsafe case does not need a check for it, which is the
cheapest kind of authorization there is.

get.summary:
`@Query()` with no argument binds the WHOLE query string to a DTO, which
the global pipe validates and transforms - so `page` really is a `number`
by the time it arrives.

`@Headers('x-request-id')` still binds a single header. Header names are
case-insensitive per the HTTP spec and Node lowercases them, so always match
in lowercase. Phase 18 replaces this with a proper correlation id generated
by middleware and attached to every log line.

`@Param('id', ParseObjectIdPipe)` - a pipe bound to ONE ARGUMENT, the
tightest of the four scopes.

Without it, `GET /users/not-an-id` reaches Mongoose, throws a CastError and
becomes a 500: a client's typo recorded as a server error. With it, the
request is rejected with 400 before any service code runs.

Note pipes run AFTER guards, so from Phase 8 an unauthenticated caller is
turned away before we spend anything validating their input.

put.summary:
PUT on a SUB-RESOURCE: "set this user's role to exactly this" is genuinely
idempotent, which is what PUT means. Modelling one meaningful state change
as its own sub-resource beats a generic PATCH, because it documents intent
and can carry its own authorization rule - Phase 8 puts `@Roles(ADMIN)` on
this route alone while leaving profile edits open to the owner.

get.summary:
===========================================================================
LIST - SCOPED TO THE CALLER. This is an authorization boundary.
===========================================================================
THE BUG THIS FIXES: `memberId` used to be taken straight from the query
string, so omitting it returned EVERY project in the database. A brand-new
user with no projects could read the entire organisation's project list.

That is BROKEN OBJECT-LEVEL AUTHORIZATION (OWASP API1), and the shape of
the mistake is worth recognising because it is extremely common:

    GET /projects/:id   was guarded by ProjectAccessGuard   ✓
    GET /projects       was not guarded at all              ✗

Guarding the item route feels like the job is done - but a collection
endpoint ENUMERATES the very things the item guard protects. A guard on
`/:id` stops you reading one project you should not see; it does nothing
about a list that hands you all of them.

WHY A GUARD WOULD NOT WORK HERE, and this is the interesting part:
`ProjectAccessGuard` answers "may this user touch THIS project?" and needs
an id from the route. A list has no id. Collection authorization is not a
yes/no decision - it is a FILTER, and a filter has to live in the query.

So the rule is: scope the query by identity from the TOKEN, never from a
client-supplied parameter.

INTERVIEW: "you guarded /:id - why is the list still a problem?" This is
the answer, and it separates people who have thought about authorization
from people who have added a guard.
===========================================================================

READ requires MEMBERSHIP - any project role will do.

The guard is applied per route rather than to the class, because `POST
/projects` and `GET /projects` have no project to check yet.

patch.summary: WRITE requires the MANAGER role WITHIN this project.

post.summary:
`@HttpCode(200)` because POST defaults to 201 Created, and this creates
nothing - it transitions an existing resource. 201 would tell a client (and
a caching proxy) that a new resource exists somewhere, which is untrue.

delete.summary:
Two route parameters, bound BY NAME - argument order is irrelevant.

Returns the updated project rather than 204, because the client needs the
new member list to re-render. "204 for every DELETE" is a convention, not a
rule; returning the affected resource saves a round trip.

get.summary:
===========================================================================
SERVER-SENT EVENTS
===========================================================================
`@Sse()` makes Nest hold the response open, set
`Content-Type: text/event-stream`, and write each emitted value in the SSE
wire format:

    id: 65f1...
    event: notification
    data: {"id":"65f1...","title":"WEB-142 assigned to you"}
    <blank line>

THE HANDLER RETURNS AN OBSERVABLE THAT NEVER COMPLETES. That is the whole
reason Nest models responses as Observables rather than Promises (Phase 9)
- a promise resolves once and the connection would close.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------
SSE vs WEBSOCKETS - the decision, not the trivia
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
                       SSE                      WebSocket
  Direction            server -> client only    bidirectional
  Protocol             plain HTTP               upgrade to ws://
  Reconnection         AUTOMATIC, built in      you write it
  Proxies / corporate  works (it is just HTTP)  often blocked
  HTTP/2 multiplexing  yes                      no (own connection)
  Auth                 awkward - see below      handshake payload
  Binary               no (text only)           yes
  Browser conn. limit  6 per origin on HTTP/1.1 not affected

DEFAULT TO SSE for server->client push. It is less code, it survives
corporate proxies, and the browser reconnects for you with backoff - which
is the part people underestimate, because reconnection logic is where
hand-rolled WebSocket clients go wrong.

REACH FOR WEBSOCKETS when the client must send a stream too: chat,
collaborative editing, presence, live cursors. Notifications are one-way,
so SSE is the right default here - and the gateway in this module exists
because typing indicators and presence are genuinely bidirectional.

THE HTTP/1.1 SIX-CONNECTION LIMIT is the one real SSE gotcha: a browser
allows six connections per origin, and an open SSE stream holds one. Open a
few tabs and the app stops loading images. HTTP/2 removes it entirely
(multiplexed), which in practice means "make sure production is HTTP/2".
===========================================================================

post.summary:
Creating a task requires membership of the project named in the BODY.

ProjectAccessGuard looks in params, body and query for a projectId - which
is what lets one guard serve route shapes as different as
POST /tasks { projectId } and GET /projects/:id/....

parameters.name: overdue
parameters.description:
HTTP has no booleans - `?overdue=true` arrives as the STRING "true".

`@Type(() => Boolean)` is NOT enough on its own: `Boolean("false")` is
`true`, because any non-empty string is truthy. That trap catches people
constantly, so the conversion is explicit here.

get.summary:
===========================================================================
LIST - SCOPED TO PROJECTS THE CALLER BELONGS TO
===========================================================================
THE BUG THIS FIXES: this endpoint used to pass the query straight to the
repository with no membership constraint, so ANY authenticated user could
read EVERY task in the database. Reproduced before the fix: a brand-new
account with zero projects saw another user's three tasks.

`POST /tasks` was already guarded by `ProjectAccessGuard` (it has a
projectId in the body to check). `GET /tasks` was not, because a list has
no id for a guard to check - and that asymmetry is exactly where
collection-level authorization gets forgotten.

A LIST IS AUTHORIZED BY FILTERING, NOT BY A YES/NO GUARD. The scope is
derived from the token and passed to the repository as a constraint that
the caller cannot influence.
===========================================================================
Declared BEFORE `:id`. See the note above.

delete.summary:
Returns a small body rather than 204, because "how many comments went with
it?" is genuinely useful after a cascading delete - and it is the visible
evidence that the transaction did both halves.

patch.summary:
A dedicated endpoint for the state transition rather than a generic PATCH,
because the transition carries its own rule (the conditional update) and
will carry its own authorization rule in Phase 8.

parameters.name: overdue
parameters.description:
HTTP has no booleans - `?overdue=true` arrives as the STRING "true".

`@Type(() => Boolean)` is NOT enough on its own: `Boolean("false")` is
`true`, because any non-empty string is truthy. That trap catches people
constantly, so the conversion is explicit here.

delete.summary:
===========================================================================
DELETE A COMMENT - nested under its task, which is where it belongs
===========================================================================
Comments are already created and listed under `/tasks/:id/comments`. The
standalone `DELETE /comments/:id` was the odd one out, and that anomaly is
precisely what made it hard to authorize: a bare comment id gives you no
route to the project that owns the membership rule.

Nesting it fixes both problems at once:
  - the URL is consistent with create and list
  - `TaskAccessGuard` establishes project membership from `:id` BEFORE the
    handler runs, so the service only has to decide the moderation rule

NOTE it is NOT decorated with `@ProjectRoles(Role.MANAGER)`. Any member may
reach this route, because the AUTHOR of a comment is usually an ordinary
member deleting their own. The finer rule - author, or manager, or global
admin - needs the comment itself, so it lives in the service.

That split is worth naming: a GUARD answers "may you touch this resource
at all?", and the SERVICE answers "may you do this particular thing to it?".
Pushing the second into a guard means loading the comment twice.
===========================================================================

info.title: TaskFlow API
info.description:
A production-style NestJS modular monolith: users, projects, tasks, comments,
notifications, background jobs and real-time delivery.

**Authentication.** Every endpoint requires a bearer access token unless it is
marked otherwise. Obtain one from `POST /auth/register` or `POST /auth/login`,
then use the **Authorize** button above.

**Refresh tokens** are delivered as an httpOnly cookie and are not visible to
JavaScript - which is deliberate (see the Phase 7 notes in the repository).

email.description:
`@Transform` runs BEFORE validation, so the value is normalised first.

Trimming and lowercasing at the edge means the rest of the system never has
to think about `" Ada@Example.com "`. The schema lowercases too - belt and
braces, and the schema is what makes the unique index meaningful.

password.description: Plaintext, received once over TLS, hashed immediately, never stored or logged.

NOTE: no `@IsStrongPassword()` here, deliberately.

Login validates CREDENTIALS, not password policy. Applying the strength
rules would (a) reject users whose password predates a policy change, and
(b) leak the policy to anyone probing the endpoint. Validate the shape
minimally on login; enforce the policy where the password is SET.

refreshToken.description:
Optional in the body, because the refresh token normally arrives in an
httpOnly cookie. The body form exists for non-browser clients (mobile,
CLI, service-to-service) which have no cookie jar.

Supporting both is the pragmatic choice; the cookie is the SAFER one for
browsers - see the note in auth.controller.ts.

role.description:
Optional. Defaults to MEMBER in the service.

SECURITY NOTE: accepting a role from the request body is only safe because
Phase 8 puts `@Roles(Role.ADMIN)` on this endpoint. Self-registration
(Phase 7) must IGNORE this field and force MEMBER - otherwise anyone can
sign up as an admin. That is the single most common privilege-escalation
bug in tutorial-grade APIs, and `whitelist: true` alone does NOT prevent it,
because `role` IS on the allow-list here. The protection is the guard plus
a separate, narrower DTO for registration.

userId.description:
`@IsMongoId()` rejects a malformed id at the edge with 400, instead of
letting it reach Mongoose and become a `CastError` -> 500. Same job as
`ParseObjectIdPipe`, applied to a body field rather than a route param.

role.description: The member's role WITHIN this project - not their global role.

key.description:
`@Matches` with an anchored pattern. Note the ORDER of decorators does not
matter to class-validator (all rules run and all failures are collected),
but the order of `@Transform` vs validation DOES: transforms run first.

members.description:
PHASE 7 REMOVED  FROM THIS DTO.

It used to be a body field. Now the owner is the AUTHENTICATED CALLER,
read from the JWT via @CurrentUser(). The rule that motivated the change:

    Identity comes from the token, never from the payload.

Any field that determines ownership or permission and is accepted from a
request body is a privilege-escalation vector - a client could create a
project owned by someone else, and once membership drives access, grant
themselves a way into another team data.

dueDate.description:
`@IsDateString()` validates an ISO-8601 STRING and leaves it a string; the
service converts to a `Date`.

WHY NOT `@Type(() => Date)`? Because it accepts anything `new Date()`
accepts, including `"yesterday"` -> `Invalid Date`, which then silently
writes `null` or throws deep in the driver. Validating the FORMAT first and
converting explicitly afterwards fails loudly at the edge instead.
